items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: I joined Count Basie in 1938 and he used to do like three hundred one-nighters a year

ctx.x: Is it a skill that you learned — how did you learn that skill? Can you describe that?

Yes, because in my era, as you know, there was a lot of prejudice toward the musicians because we couldn’t play in a studio band, they had radio bands that were getting paid weekly, they were on a salary. They had musicians here at Fox Studio, MGM, Metro Goldwyn Mayer, they were all on staff. And they got paid whenever they worked or played. But they didn’t have black musicians at the time. So our only course was to play solos. And when you picked up your horn, you’d get you a “Georgia Brown” or something,…

to do. They could be with their families, you know? But we had to take to the road. And as I was telling Wynton Marsalis, I made a CD with him last week. And I told him that you know there were quite a few good, legitimate trumpet players years ago, but they had no place to play. There was one guy, Russell Smith, he was the greatest student Bach had. He learned the trumpet, oh there was no kind of concert trumpet he couldn’t play. But he couldn’t get a job. So he had to go with Fletcher Henderson for the rest of…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And Jo Jones and Walter Page recommended me to the Basie band, and that was my beginning of a career with Count Basie.

ctx.x: Yeah, because we never got to see each other too much anyway. Of course when I joined Count Basie’s band in 1938…when I first went to New York and joined Lucky Millinder’s band and Lucky had a good band and I enjoyed playing…he had Don Byas in the band, he had Charlie Shavers, Billy Kyle who later joined Louis Armstrong and…oh he had a good band, Walter Johnson was on drums, wonderful drummer. And some reason or the other, Lucky fired me for Dizzy and that’s when I went with Basie’s band because I had played with…

Before we get too far into Count Basie, one question before we leave your early background: you said your uncle had taught you the scales, the trumpet. How did you actually learn to read music, was that from him as well, or…?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: That was the greatest thrill of my life, being a member of Count Basie's aggregation.

ctx.x: you know. But Buck was the favorite, you know. It didn't make any difference to me who took the solo. That's one thing about Basie's band, it didn't matter who played the solo, just so you got to play, you know. And if you didn't swing, you wouldn't have a solo, anyway. They'd take it away from you and give it to somebody else. Pres would ring a bell that he used to have, if it wasn't swing he'd ring this bell, you know. That was the cue that that wasn't the solo for you; give it to somebody else.
And, gee whiz, what a thrill it was to play with that band. That was the greatest thrill of my life, being a member of Count Basie's aggregation.
